summary: Defines MIB textual conventions for representing commonly used network-layer addressing information, such as IP addresses. Reusing them keeps different MIB modules consistent. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 3291.

eli5.summary: When many people write down addresses they should use the same format. This defines that shared format for network management data.

questions: mib textual conventions for ip addresses
how to represent ipv6 in snmp mib
subtitle: Standard building blocks for managing IP addresses across IPv4, IPv6, and DNS.

tldr.problem: Old MIB modules used a limited IPv4-only address type that could not represent IPv6 addresses or DNS names. When IPv6 arrived, those MIBs became inadequate.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2851 defines reusable textual conventions that bundle two objects: an InetAddressType (saying whether the address is IPv4, IPv6, or a DNS name) and an InetAddress (holding the actual bits). Designers can import these conventions rather than inventing their own.
tldr.outcome: The standard succeeded but was replaced by RFC 3291 with a slightly enhanced design. The core idea—a flexible pair of type and value—became the foundation for modern network management.

today: RFC 3291 superseded this standard in 2002 with enhancements to IPv6 scope handling and address type extensibility. Both RFCs use the same core design principle: a type-value pair that lets MIB modules represent any internet address.

sections.title: The Problem with IpAddress
sections.content:
For years, network management used SNMP's IpAddress data type, which could only hold a 4-byte IPv4 address. The arrival of IPv6, with its 16-byte addresses, exposed a gap: existing MIB modules that used IpAddress could not represent IPv6 at all. Some systems were multi-homed or used DNS names instead of IP addresses. There was no standard way for MIB writers to handle all these cases.

RFC 2851 solves this by defining textual conventions—standardized building blocks that MIB authors can reuse instead of inventing their own ad-hoc solutions. This keeps different MIB modules consistent and interoperable.
sections.eli5: Old management tools could only write down IPv4 addresses. When IPv6 arrived, they had no way to represent those addresses. This RFC gives everyone a shared template so they all write addresses the same way.

sections.title: The Core Design: Type Plus Value
sections.content:
The solution uses a pair of objects: InetAddressType and InetAddress. The type object is an enumeration that says what kind of address follows (ipv4, ipv6, or dns). The address object holds the raw bytes. Together, they allow a MIB to represent any internet address type the designer needs.

For IPv4, InetAddressIPv4 is 4 octets in network byte order, displayed as 1d.1d.1d.1d (dotted notation). For IPv6, InetAddressIPv6 is 16 octets plus an optional 4-byte scope identifier (used for link-local and site-local addresses to disambiguate identical addresses on different links). For DNS names, InetAddressDNS is up to 255 octets as a character string.

The scope identifier is crucial for IPv6: link-local addresses like fe80::1 are not globally unique; you must also know which interface (link) they are on. The scope field holds that interface index.
sections.eli5: Every address comes in two parts: first, a tag saying what type it is (IPv4, IPv6, or a name), then the address itself. That way you always know how to read it.

sections.title: Using Textual Conventions in a MIB
sections.content:
When a MIB designer defines a table to track peers or routes, they no longer invent their own address fields. Instead, they use the pair: immediately before each InetAddress, they place an InetAddressType object with the last sub-identifier one less than the address object's. The SNMP engine then knows the type determines how to interpret the value.

Table indexing with these conventions works because the type and address pair form a meaningful ordering. A management application can query for addresses of a single type, or a specific type and address prefix. The RFC includes an example MIB with a peer table indexed by address type and address, and shows compliance statements that let implementations declare which address types they support (for example, IPv4 only, or IPv4 and global IPv6).

A critical constraint: do not subtype these conventions in object definitions. Subtypes bind the MIB to specific address formats and break future extensions. Compliance statements are the right place to express restrictions.
sections.eli5: When you build a table in your network management system, you put down the type first, then the address. Other tools know to read the type first so they understand what the address means.

sections.title: IPv6 Scopes and DNS Resolution
sections.content:
IPv6 link-local and site-local addresses require a scope identifier because the same address value can appear on many different links. RFC 2851 defines the scope as a 4-byte value (matching sockaddr_in6 from RFC 2553) that typically holds the interface index. Global IPv6 addresses do not include a scope. When a scope identifier is zero, it refers to the default scope—used when the real scope is not known, though this should be a last resort.

DNS names add a temporal dimension: when should they be resolved? The RFC says the DESCRIPTION of any MIB object that might hold a DNS name MUST state whether the resolution happens once (when the object is written) or repeatedly (each time the name is used). The description must also say whether reverse lookups are performed and when.
sections.eli5: IPv6 addresses on the same link look identical, so you need to know which link. DNS names don't have one fixed address, so the MIB writer must explain when to look up a name.
